findings.finding: The plan says the ledger anchor is the 'first parent of all replayed commits'. The code does not support this. Only commits whose original parent is the boundary map to `ledger_anchor_sha`. Other replayed commits keep their own replayed parents, and any other out-of-range parent maps to `current_tip`. All replayed commits do descend from the anchor, so carrying the signed bytes still propagates. The reasoning should not rely on the stronger claim.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace '(first parent of all replayed commits)' with '(the rewritten parent of the boundary's children, and so an ancestor of every replayed commit)'.

findings.finding: The ledger re-sign is described as building a DSSE envelope from scratch ('`signature` = DSSE over `authorship.build_authorship_statement(event_uuid, content_hash)`'). The plan names no signing or encoding function for it, and it also says nothing about how the raw path's `sign_event_authorship` envelope becomes the stored `author_sig` string. The codebase already has both halves. `authorship.sign_authorship(payload, key_path, principal)` does the PAE + `sshsig.sign` + `Envelope`, and `sign_event_authorship` is just `canonical_str(build_authorship_statement(...))` passed to `sign_authorship`. `_seam._apply_authorship` turns an envelope into the stored string with `dsse.encode(envelope.payload_type, envelope.payload, [{keyid, sig}])`. That string is the format `compact_txn._build_authorship_ledger` copies verbatim into the ledger `signature` field (`"signature": sig` from `ev.get("author_sig")`).
scenarios: An implementer hand-builds the ledger DSSE (a different payload serialization, a missing `keyid=principal`, or a different envelope encoding). The signature is then not byte-compatible with what `_ledger_events` hands to the verifier, so the 6,070 ledger targets still fail.
The raw path stores the `Envelope` object, or an encoding that differs from `_seam`'s, as `author_sig`.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a small `_encode(envelope)` helper in `reclaim_resign.py` that mirrors `_seam._apply_authorship` (`dsse.encode(env.payload_type, env.payload, [{"keyid": s.keyid, "sig": s.sig} for s in env.signatures])`), or pull the existing lines out into a shared helper. Use it for both raw `author_sig` and ledger `signature`, and produce the ledger envelope with `authorship.sign_authorship` over the canonical Statement bytes.

findings.finding: The unit tests exercise only unsigned raw events and a ledger entry with signer_pubkey: null. The dominant real inputs are not covered: 1,435 raw events and 6,070 ledger entries that already carry a signature from an off-keyring key. Three of the plan's own mechanisms also have no isolating test: the subtle below-boundary rule ('added_at <= position'); the anchor-commit/checkpoint inline overrides in _write_base; and the .retired rename and merge paths in _diff_lines.
scenarios: sign_event_authorship appends to, or fails to replace, an existing foreign signature. Unit tests stay green; the real-data run fails or produces double-signed events.
A key valid at the anchor commit but with added_at > position is chosen for a below-boundary event. It passes before the collapse and fails after, and no unit test catches it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the agent fixture skip when a per-process socket ssh-agent cannot be started (e.g. Windows / `ssh-agent -a` fails), not only when the binary is absent.

findings.finding: The test fixture 'loaded into an ssh-agent the fixture starts and kills' is skipped only 'without ssh-agent or ssh-keygen >= 8.9'. Win32-OpenSSH ships an ssh-agent binary that runs as a Windows service over a named pipe, not as a per-process unix-socket agent. The skip predicate is therefore satisfied and the fixture errors instead of skipping.
findings.location: Testing: 'loaded into an ssh-agent the fixture starts and kills; skipped without ssh-agent or ssh-keygen >= 8.9'
scenarios: Windows developer workstation or Windows CI runner. The ssh-agent and ssh-keygen 9.x binaries are present, so the test is not skipped; starting a socket agent fails and the fixture raises. test_reclaim_resign.py errors and `make verify` fails.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap agent startup in the fixture. If launching `ssh-agent -a <tmp sock>` fails or the platform is Windows, call pytest.skip with a reason, rather than gating solely on shutil.which('ssh-agent').

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] For events below the boundary, model the collapsed era exactly: a key added and/or revoked below the boundary counts as added iff `added_at <= position`, and as revoked iff `revoked_at <= position`, ignoring original-graph ancestry. Add a test with a key revoked on a concurrent branch below the boundary.
evidence: attest/authorship.py:189-202: `if added_commit == anchor_commit and anchor_position is not None: added = added_at <= anchor_position` … `if revoked_commit == anchor_commit and anchor_position is not None: revoked = revoked_at <= anchor_position`
The plan text constrains only `added_at`; it says nothing about `revoked_at`
findings.finding: The plan's rule for the boundary reproduces only half of the verifier's within-commit ordering. Its premise is that collapsing below-boundary commits into the checkpoint only changes how `added_at` is ordered against the event's position. `keys_valid_at_anchor` also orders `revoked_at` by position when the revoke commit equals the anchor commit (lines 196-202). Suppose a key was revoked below the boundary in a commit that was NOT an ancestor of the event's commit (a concurrent branch), with `revoked_at <= position`. On the original graph it is valid; after the collapse both resolve to the checkpoint and it is revoked. The plan can then pick it, and the re-signed event fails. The reverse mismatch also exists: a key added below the boundary in a concurrent commit (not an ancestor on the original graph) with `added_at <= position` becomes valid after the collapse. The plan rejects it, which can cause avoidable 'no key' ResignErrors.
findings.location: Approach §1 Key choice ('If that commit is an ancestor of the boundary, a key added below the boundary must also satisfy `added_at <= position`')
scenarios: A bot key was rotated on a concurrent tickets-branch line below the boundary. An event below the boundary, with a later timestamp than the revoke, gets re-signed with the revoked key and comes out as key_not_valid_at_era after the collapse.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the resolver so every position whose commit is in `rev-list <boundary>` maps to one synthetic 'checkpoint' sha. Map the anchor of each below-boundary event to that sha too, and make is_ancestor(checkpoint, X) true for every replayed X. `keys_valid_at_anchor` then applies its own position ordering to adds and revokes alike.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve each event's era against the rewritten parent mapping, not the original graph. At minimum, before moving the branch, check every re-signed target against the scratch ref with the verifier's resolvers. Add a test where a parent below the boundary gets re-parented.
evidence: reclaim_collapse.py:514-523: `if parent == self.boundary: mapped = self.ledger_anchor_sha else: mapped = self.old_to_new.get(parent); if mapped is None and parent not in in_range: mapped = self.current_tip`
old_to_new holds only boundary→checkpoint and the replayed commits, so any other below-boundary parent hits the current_tip fallback
The plan's only adjustment for the collapse covers events whose commit is an ancestor of the boundary
findings.finding: Key choice is computed 'on the ORIGINAL graph', on the premise that only below-boundary commits change ancestry. In `_StreamedRewrite._replay`, any parent that is outside the range and is not the boundary itself is re-parented to `self.current_tip`, the previously replayed commit in topo order (reclaim_collapse.py:518-519). That covers a below-boundary non-boundary commit, such as a side branch forked before the boundary and merged after it. An above-boundary commit then gains ancestors it lacked in the original graph. A KEY_REVOKE (or KEY_ADD) commit can therefore become an ancestor of an event commit in the rewritten history, changing which keys the verifier accepts compared with the plan's choice.
findings.location: Approach §1 Key choice ('reuses `attest.authorship.keys_valid_at_anchor` on the ORIGINAL graph … anchored at the event's introducing commit')
scenarios: A writer committed on a stale parent from before the boundary and the commit landed above it. The commit is re-parented onto whatever was replayed just before, which may include a revoke of the key the plan chose for that writer's events.
findings.suggested_fix: Before moving the branch in collapse_shadow_tracker, run the verifier's era check (`build_event_commit_maps` + `build_ancestry_oracle` against the scratch ref) for every target, and raise ResignError on any non-verified target. Alternatively, compute key choice after a dry-run collapse, using the rewritten graph.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Choose each target's key using the validity the REWRITTEN graph will give, covering revocations as well as adds and the re-parenting of parents outside the range, not the original graph plus an add-only correction.
evidence: Plan: "Key choice reuses attest.authorship.keys_valid_at_anchor on the ORIGINAL graph ... If that commit is an ancestor of the boundary, a key added below the boundary must also satisfy added_at <= position". The plan says nothing about revoked_at.
src/rebar/attest/authorship.py:196-202: revoked iff revoked_at <= anchor_position when revoked_commit == anchor_commit, otherwise by ancestry.

src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:518-519: `if mapped is None and parent not in in_range: mapped = self.current_tip` — parents outside the range are re-attached to the current tip, which enlarges ancestry.
The operator decision mentions using 'the bot key that was on 594c's keyring when it was written', which suggests key rotation, so revocations are likely in the real keyring.
findings.finding: Key selection is worked out on the ORIGINAL graph with only one correction (added_at <= position for adds below the boundary). The rewritten graph that verify-identity actually checks differs in ways the plan doesn't model: (1) revocations below the boundary also collapse to the checkpoint and are ordered by position (keys_valid_at_anchor: revoked iff revoked_at <= anchor_position when revoked_commit == anchor_commit), and the plan has no matching revoked_at rule; (2) _replay maps every parent outside the range to self.current_tip, so a side-branch commit that forked below the boundary becomes a descendant of mainline commits it was not originally descended from. A key revoked on the mainline (above the boundary, or below it, where it collapses to the checkpoint) can then be an ancestor of the event's rewritten commit. In both cases the plan picks a key that passes on the original graph but is key_not_valid_at_era after the collapse.
scenarios: Key K1 revoked at position R below the boundary, on a commit that is not an ancestor of an event E at a later position P > R introduced on a sibling commit that is also below the boundary. On the original graph K1 is valid for E; after the collapse both resolve to the checkpoint, R <= P, so K1 counts as revoked and E fails verification.

An event introduced on a side branch that forked below the boundary and merged above it, while key K was revoked on the mainline before that side commit was replayed. On the original graph K is valid; in the rewritten graph the revoke commit is an ancestor, so the event fails.

A KEY_ADD event file deleted below the boundary leaves no add record in the collapsed history, so its added_at cannot be resolved and the key is valid for nothing. The original-graph check would not notice.
findings.suggested_fix: Work out key validity against the collapsed topology. First run a collapse without re-signing to the dry-run ref (signing changes only blob bytes, so the commit topology and old->new mapping are identical). Then build position_map and is_ancestor from that ref and anchor each target at its mapped commit (checkpoint for below-boundary ledger entries, old_to_new for others). Call keys_valid_at_anchor with those resolvers. This handles adds, revokes, re-parenting and deleted KEY_ADD files with one rule instead of hand-written corrections.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Handle build_ancestry_oracle(shadow) returning None, either by falling back to reclaim_collapse._is_ancestor(shadow, a, d) or by raising ResignError.
evidence: src/rebar/attest/authorship_resolution.py:340-363: `def build_ancestry_oracle(tracker: str) -> Callable[[str, str], bool] | None` ... 'Returns None when the graph cannot be read; callers then keep their subprocess path.'
findings.finding: The plan uses authorship.build_ancestry_oracle(shadow) as the is_ancestor resolver, but that function returns None when it cannot read the graph. Callers are expected to fall back to a subprocess. The plan does not define that fallback, and passing None to keys_valid_at_anchor would raise a TypeError instead of a ResignError.
scenarios: The shadow's `git rev-list --parents HEAD` times out (300s) on the full history, so the oracle is None and plan construction crashes with a non-ResignError exception.
findings.suggested_fix: is_ancestor = authorship.build_ancestry_oracle(str(shadow)) or (lambda a, d: reclaim_collapse._is_ancestor(Path(shadow), a, d))

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Before implementing, add a spike step: run keys_valid_at_anchor against the original graph for all 8,379 failing events, list the distinct keyring keys needed, and confirm each private half can be loaded into the run principal's ssh-agent; if one cannot, record the operator decision for those events.
evidence: Plan: "key_files maps keyring public-key text to a public-key file whose private half is held by the ssh-agent at SSH_AUTH_SOCK"
Plan: "The supplied passing key with the latest added_at is used. None: ResignError with the count, before signing."
AC provenance: "principal=RebarBotNava; privilege_posture=narrower". Nothing says this principal holds the older bot keys' private material.
Evidence class: Unverified. Nothing in the plan or repo inventories which keyring keys the 8,379 events (1,500-era to current) need, or whether their private halves can be obtained.
findings.finding: The plan assumes the operator's ssh-agent can hold the private half of every bot key that was on 594c's keyring at each failing event's era, but it never establishes that those historical private keys still exist or are available to the run principal. Any that were rotated away, revoked, or destroyed cannot be used. The plan's own design makes the whole run fail if even one era lacks a usable key.
findings.location: Approach §1 (key_files / Key choice / Pre-flight); last two [non-codebase] ACs
scenarios: Events from an early era are only valid under a bot key that has since been revoked and its private key deleted: keys_valid_at_anchor returns only that key, the supplied set has no passing key, and the run raises ResignError with no way to fix it.
RebarBotNava (narrower posture) only has the current bot key, so the real-data AC can never pass.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a pre-implementation spike to Approach (or a prerequisite ticket): a read-only script that groups the failing events by the set of keyring keys valid at each anchor and reports any group whose valid keys have no private material available. Make its result (all groups covered) a gating precondition stated in Context.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that a failed post-sign verification (raw via verify_authorship_any_key, and an equivalent check for ledger DSSE entries) raises ResignError naming the target — fatal for the run, retryable after fixing the cause — before any ref is written.

Ledger branch: 'signature = DSSE over ... signer_pubkey = chosen key' — no verification step named
findings.finding: The post-sign self-check ('check with authorship.verify_authorship_any_key') is a new failure arm with no stated disposition. Every other arm says it raises ResignError, but the plan never says what happens when a freshly produced signature fails this check. There is also no equivalent check for re-signed ledger entries (DSSE signature plus signer_pubkey).
findings.location: Approach §1 Pre-flight: 'serialize with canonical_bytes, check with authorship.verify_authorship_any_key'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Build the uuid→target index in `build_resign_plan` from `verify_authorship._collect_all(str(shadow))` (raw = `_ScopedEvent` with `event` set; ledger = `_ledger_events` entries) instead of re-scanning event files and SNAPSHOT ledgers by hand.
evidence: Plan: 'a uuid naming an active raw event file `<ticket>/<ts>-<uuid>-<TYPE>.json` at the tip is a raw target … Otherwise it is looked up in the `authorship_ledger` of active SNAPSHOTs at the tip'
Plan: 'Position: raw `{timestamp}-{uuid}` (as `verify_authorship._event_from_file`); ledger `position.position`'

src/rebar/_commands/verify_authorship.py:372 `_collect_all(tracker)` walks ticket dirs, skips `_is_gate_exempt_ticket`/`_is_archived_ticket`, and calls `_event_from_file`, which expands SNAPSHOTs through `_ledger_events` (line 303) and builds `position = f"{event.get('timestamp')}-{event.get('uuid')}"` (line 356)
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:172 confirms the shadow is a git worktree, so a filesystem collector can read the tip
findings.finding: The target-matching step re-implements the verifier's own event enumeration. It looks for active raw event files `<ticket>/<ts>-<uuid>-<TYPE>.json` and `authorship_ledger` entries in active SNAPSHOTs, and computes positions 'as verify_authorship._event_from_file'. `verify_authorship._collect_all(tracker)` already does all of this through `_active_event_files` (with `is_active_event`), `_event_from_file` and `_ledger_events`. It returns `_ScopedEvent`s carrying `event_uuid`, `ticket_id`, `position`, `commit_sha`, `event`, `ticket_dir`, `signer_pubkey` and `content_hash`, and it applies the same gate-exempt/archived skips the enforced run used to produce `failing`. The shadow is a git worktree reset to the tip (`_assert_shadow_tracker` checks `--is-inside-work-tree`), so the collector can run on it directly.
scenarios: A hand-written matcher handles retired `.json.retired` files, dot-files, sidecar event types (`KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES` filter) or archived tickets differently from the verifier. A uuid the verifier reported then either fails to match (spurious `ResignError`) or matches a different file than the one the verifier checked.
Later changes to how the verifier enumerates events (new exemptions, ledger shape) are not picked up by the re-sign matcher, so the two drift apart.
findings.suggested_fix: In `reclaim_resign.build_resign_plan`, call `verify_authorship._collect_all(str(shadow))` once on the tip worktree and index the result by `event_uuid`. Treat entries with `event is not None` as raw targets, taking the file path from `ticket_dir` plus the filename in `ref` and the blob id from `git ls-tree` at the tip. Treat the rest as ledger targets that keep `position` / `commit_sha` / `content_hash`. Then drop the plan's separate path-pattern and ledger-walk description.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Build the key-choice position map with the verifier's own scan (`authorship_resolution._scan_added_event_files(str(shadow))` + `_position_of`, counting `.json.retired`) instead of `_position_commit_map_for_tracker`, whose `*.json`-only walk differs from the verifier's.
evidence: reclaim_collapse.py:369-384: git log --diff-filter=A … -- "*.json" (no `*.json.retired`)
authorship_resolution.py:166-192: `_scan_added_event_files` walks `-- *.json *{_RETIRED_SUFFIX}`; its docstring: 'A reclaimed history adds below-checkpoint events directly as .json.retired'
authorship_resolution.py:265-271: build_position_commit_map, which verify_authorship._batched_resolvers uses (verify_authorship.py:443), counts .json.retired adds
attest/authorship.py:186-188: an unresolved added_at makes keys_valid_at_anchor skip the key
findings.finding: The plan uses `reclaim_collapse._position_commit_map_for_tracker(shadow)` as the position resolver for key choice, on the premise that it matches the verifier's era resolution. Its comment says it uses 'the same full-history algorithm as rebar.attest.authorship_resolution', but it does not. It walks only `-- *.json`. The verifier's `build_position_commit_map` → `_scan_added_event_files` also counts `*.json.retired` adds. That module's own docs say a reclaimed history adds events below the checkpoint directly as `.json.retired`. Any keyring `added_at`/`revoked_at` position, or event position, that only resolves through a `.retired` add returns None in the plan's resolver. `keys_valid_at_anchor` then skips that key (`added_commit is None → continue`), or misses a revocation.
findings.location: Approach §1 Key choice ('resolvers scoped to the shadow (`reclaim_collapse._position_commit_map_for_tracker(shadow)` …)')
scenarios: A tip whose history already contains a reclaimed segment, or any event or KEY_ADD that only appears as `.json.retired`: the key is wrongly treated as never added, causing a spurious 'no key' ResignError, or a revoked key is treated as live.
findings.suggested_fix: In reclaim_resign, build the map as `{_position_of(p): sha for sha, p in _scan_added_event_files(str(shadow)) if _position_of(p)}` (newest-first overwrite, so the oldest add wins). Or expose a public tracker-scoped wrapper in authorship_resolution.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State where `ResignError` and `ResignPlan` are defined and how the reclaim_resign ↔ reclaim_collapse import cycle is avoided (for example a TYPE_CHECKING-only import of ResignPlan in reclaim_collapse, with reclaim_resign defining `ResignError(ReclaimCollapseError)`), and add both modules to the Scope bullet that names the change.

Plan §2: `collapse_shadow_tracker(..., resign: ResignPlan | None = None)` and 'a shortfall raises `ResignError`'

The plan does not say which module defines ResignError, or how the import cycle is avoided.

If ResignError is not a ReclaimCollapseError subclass, existing `except ReclaimCollapseError` handlers (cli, reclaim_dry_run) do not catch it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say that the two new CollapseResult fields also show up in `reclaim-collapse --format json` output (through to_dict), and either accept that and say so, or keep them out of to_dict when resign is None; then make clear that 'byte for byte' refers to the rewritten tree and commits.

src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:154-155 — `print(js_safe_dumps(result.to_dict()))`
Plan: "`None` keeps today's output byte for byte" and "No CLI flag, config key or env var"
findings.finding: Adding `events_resigned` and `ledger_entries_resigned` to the `CollapseResult` dataclass changes the public `rebar reclaim-collapse --format json` output on every run, because `cli()` prints `js_safe_dumps(result.to_dict())` and `to_dict` is `asdict(self)`. This happens even when resign is None. The plan does not list the CLI JSON output as an affected consumer, and its claims that 'None keeps today's output byte for byte' and that there is 'No CLI ... ' change suggest the CLI output stays the same.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Before moving the branch, run the era check on every target against the scratch-ref result (position map and ancestry built from the scratch ref), and raise ResignError if any target is not VERIFIED, rather than only counting substitutions.
evidence: Plan: "a shortfall raises ResignError, deletes the scratch ref, leaves the branch unchanged" — the only condition checked is the count shortfall.
reclaim_collapse.py:112-121 moves the branch and runs reset --hard as soon as the stream finishes, so with no verify gate, a bad era choice becomes the branch tip.
verify_authorship._verify_signed (lines 197-220) is what decides the outcome, and it looks at the rewritten commit_sha and position resolvers that exist only after the stream.
findings.finding: The only post-rewrite safeguard before the branch moves is a count check: every raw target substituted and every ledger target re-signed. Nothing in the engine checks that the re-signed targets actually verify under the enforced era rule on the rewritten graph, which is what this work is for. Any error in key choice, anchor resolution or ledger commit_sha mapping is caught only by the out-of-repo real-data run, after the branch has already been moved (apply=True).
findings.location: Approach §2 last bullet ('Before moving the branch it checks every raw target present at the tip was substituted and every ledger target re-signed')
scenarios: A ledger entry's commit_sha is remapped to the checkpoint, but the chosen key's add commit resolves to a replayed commit. The count check passes and enforced verify fails.
findings.suggested_fix: After rewrite.run, build _position_commit_map from the scratch ref and an ancestry oracle over it. For each target, call keys_valid_at_anchor with its rewritten anchor, assert the chosen signer key is in the result, and confirm the signature with registry.verify against that single key. If any target fails, delete the scratch ref and raise ResignError.

findings.finding: The pre-flight requires each supplied key to be "listed by `ssh-add -L`" but does not say how the comparison is made. `ssh-add -L` prints `<type> <base64> <comment>`, and the comment usually differs from the keyring `public_key` text and from the .pub file. `ssh-add -L` also exits 1 when the agent holds no identities and 2 when it cannot reach the agent, and the plan maps neither case to an outcome. The repo has never used agent-backed signing, so this is a new surface.
scenarios: The keyring stores `ssh-ed25519 AAAA… bot@host-2025` while the agent lists `ssh-ed25519 AAAA… /home/x/.ssh/bot`. A whole-line string comparison reports the key missing and the pre-flight wrongly refuses the run.
SSH_AUTH_SOCK is unset in the runbook shell: `ssh-add -L` exits 2. If that is not mapped to ResignError, the failure surfaces later as an unclear CalledProcessError from ssh-keygen.
findings.suggested_fix: Normalize every key, from the keyring text, the key_files content, and each `ssh-add -L` line, to `split()[:2]` before comparing.
